name: OPA690IDBVR
title: Wideband, unity-gain-stable voltage-feedback operational amplifier with disable
summary: The OPA690 is a single bipolar-input, voltage-feedback op amp that is stable at unity gain, with 535 MHz of small-signal bandwidth at G = 1, 1900 V/µs slew rate and 215 mA of output current from 6.1 mA of supply current. It runs from 5 V to 12 V total supply, single or split, and its DIS pin powers it down to about 100 µA with a high-impedance output. It comes in an 8-pin SOIC (OPA690ID) and a 6-pin SOT-23 (OPA690IDBV); the two packages are specified separately. Typical uses are ADC drivers, video and xDSL line drivers, transimpedance stages and active filters.

circuits.title: Single-supply, gain-of-4, 5-MHz 2nd-order Butterworth low-pass filter
circuits.description: A Sallen-Key low-pass stage on one 5-V rail with a midband gain of 4 (12 dB) and a 5-MHz corner. Two 1.87-kΩ resistors bias the input node at half the supply; the signal and the gain resistor are both ac-coupled through 0.1 µF, so the bias appears at input and output and the response has a 32-kHz low-frequency corner. 137 Ω and 432 Ω with 150 pF to ground and 100 pF back from the output set the filter; 1.5 kΩ over 500 Ω sets the gain. The 150-pF capacitor is made large so it swamps the input parasitics. Measured: a maximally flat 5-MHz passband and at most 36 dB of stop-band rejection at 80 MHz, where the amplifier itself rolls off.

parts.note: to ground at the noninverting input

notes: At G = 4 on one supply the amplifier alone reaches roughly 80 MHz, and the filter component values are trimmed to suit that.

circuits.title: DC-coupled, G = 2 V/V, ±5-V specification and test circuit
circuits.description: The circuit behind the ±5-V ac specifications. The input is terminated in 50 Ω and fed through 175 Ω, which with the 25-Ω dc resistance of the 50-Ω source matches the 200 Ω seen by the inverting input for bias-current cancellation. 402-Ω feedback and gain resistors set G = 2; a 50-Ω series resistor drives a matched 50-Ω load, so the amplifier sees 100 Ω in parallel with 804 Ω. Each rail has 0.1 µF and 6.8 µF to ground, and 0.1 µF across the two supply pins improves 2nd-harmonic distortion. Swings are quoted at the pins; output powers in dBm at the 50-Ω load.
notes: The disable line is normally left open.

circuits.title: AC-coupled, G = 2 V/V, single-supply specification and test circuit
circuits.description: The circuit behind the 5-V ac specifications. Two 698-Ω resistors hold the input at 2.5 V; the signal is ac-coupled in, and 59 Ω makes the input load 50 Ω together with the divider. A 50-Ω resistor in series with the noninverting input completes the bias-current match and, with the input capacitance, rolls the response off above 500 MHz. The gain resistor is ac-coupled, so the dc gain is 1 and the 2.5-V bias also sits at the output. The load is 100 Ω returned to VS/2.
notes: Input range: up to 1.5 V from each rail, which is 2 VPP centred on midsupply; the output reaches within 1 V of either rail while delivering more than 100 mA.

circuits.title: Inverting gain of –2 V/V on ±5 V
circuits.description: An inverting stage that keeps the 50-Ω input match and the gain of the noninverting test circuit. 200 Ω and 402 Ω set the gain; 67 Ω to ground brings the input impedance to 50 Ω. With the 50-Ω source the drive impedance is 50 Ω ∥ 67 Ω = 28.6 Ω, giving a noise gain of 2.8. RB = 146 Ω, the parallel of the 228-Ω dc resistance at the inverting node and RF, cancels the bias-current error, leaving IOS × RF. A 50-Ω series resistor drives a 50-Ω load.
notes: RB below 350 Ω needs no bypass capacitor; RB must be at least 50 Ω.

circuits.title: Driving a capacitive load with noise-gain tuning
circuits.description: A gain-of-2 stage driving a capacitive load through a series resistor, with a resistor RNG from the input node to the inverting input that raises the noise gain without changing the signal gain. The higher noise gain adds phase margin, so a smaller series resistor flattens the response into a given load, at the cost of more output noise and somewhat less loop gain. The 50-Ω input is terminated in 50 Ω and fed to the noninverting input through 175 Ω; 402-Ω feedback and gain resistors set the gain.

parts.note: noise-gain tuning; value chosen for the noise gain

circuits.title: DC-coupled inverting gain of –2 V/V with output offset adjustment
circuits.description: An inverting stage, VO/VI = –RF/RG = –2, with a ±200-mV output trim. A 10-kΩ potentiometer between 5-kΩ resistors to the ±5-V rails gives an adjustable voltage, filtered by 0.1 µF, that drives a small current into the inverting node through 20 kΩ. Because that resistor is much larger than the signal-path resistors, the trim barely changes the loop gain or the frequency response. The noninverting input returns to ground through 328 Ω bypassed by 0.1 µF.

circuits.title: High-speed DAC transimpedance amplifier
circuits.description: A current-output DAC feeds one of its complementary outputs into the inverting summing junction, and the amplifier converts it to a voltage, VO = IO × RF; the unused output goes to ground. The DAC output capacitance CD puts a zero in the noise gain that would cause peaking, so CF across RF compensates it. The noninverting input returns to ground through 50 Ω; a DAC that needs a compliance voltage other than ground can have that voltage applied there instead.

parts.note: complementary current outputs IO and IOB
feedback capacitor; sets the feedback pole for a flat response

circuits.title: High-power coax line driver on a single 12-V supply
circuits.description: An inverting stage on one 12-V rail driving a 50-Ω line: 8 VPP at the amplifier output, 4 VPP at the 50-Ω load, a gain of 8 to the output and 4 to the load. A 2-kΩ/2-kΩ divider with 0.1 µF holds the noninverting input at half the supply. The 1-VPP signal from a 50-Ω source is ac-coupled through 50 Ω into the inverting input; 400 Ω sets the gain and 5 pF across it trims the bandwidth. The output reaches the line through a 50-Ω back-match and a coupling capacitor.

operation.text: The input stage places its transconductance stage between a pair of input buffers, whose output currents carry the signal forward, instead of steering a fixed bias current into the compensation capacitor. That gives 1900 V/µs at 6.1 mA of supply current, at the price of somewhat more input voltage noise than other wideband input stages. The process is a high-speed complementary bipolar one.

The ±5-V specifications come from the dc-coupled G = 2 circuit: 50-Ω input termination, a 50-Ω series output resistor into a 50-Ω load, total load 100 Ω ∥ 804 Ω. Voltage swings are measured at the pins and output powers (dBm) at the matched load. The 175-Ω resistor in series with the noninverting input plus the 25-Ω dc source resistance equals the 200 Ω at the inverting input. A 0.1-µF capacitor across the two supply pins, in addition to the usual decoupling, typically improves 2nd-harmonic distortion on a real board.

The part is not rail-to-rail but needs little headroom: on 5 V it gives 3 VPP output with more than 120 MHz of bandwidth. The input must stay at least 1.5 V from either rail (2 VPP about midsupply) and the output at least 1 V, while still delivering more than 100 mA. The 5-V specifications use the ac-coupled circuit with a 698-Ω/698-Ω midpoint divider, a 50-Ω resistor in series with the noninverting input (the minimum value recommended; with the input capacitance it also rolls off the response above 500 MHz) and an ac-coupled gain resistor for unity dc gain. The output stage drives the 100-Ω midpoint load with little crossover distortion.

Every pin has ESD diodes to both supplies; the small-geometry transistors have low junction breakdowns, which the absolute maximum ratings reflect. The diodes also give some protection against inputs beyond the rails and carry about 10 mA continuously. Where more current is possible, for example when parts on ±15 V drive the inputs, add series current-limiting resistors in both inputs, as small as possible since they cost noise and bandwidth.

With DIS unconnected the amplifier runs normally; pulling DIS low disables it, dropping supply current to about 100 µA and putting the output and inputs into a high-impedance state. The disabled supply current is only what the disable control circuit itself draws. Turn-on is faster than turn-off (make-before-break), which suits channel multiplexing. At a gain of 1 the disabled output impedance is very high and isolation excellent; at higher noninverting gains the output looks back into RF + RG but forward and reverse isolation stay high; an inverting stage isolates poorly because RF + RG still links input to output.

Bandwidth falls as gain rises. GBP/NG predicts it only near 90° phase margin, at high gains; the part is compensated for a slightly peaked G = 2 response of 220 MHz, well above 300 MHz/2. For a flatter G = 2 response, raise the noise gain to 2.5 without changing signal gain, for example with 804 Ω across the inputs of the dc-coupled test circuit. A follower made with 402-Ω feedback and 402 Ω across the inputs responds like the G = 2 circuit; a smaller resistor across the inputs limits bandwidth further.

In an inverting stage RG is part of the input impedance. For G = –2 with RG = 50 Ω as the termination, RF is 100 Ω, the noise gain with a 50-Ω source is 2 and the output also carries the 100-Ω feedback load. Keeping RF within 200 Ω to 1.5 kΩ means larger RF and RG plus a shunt resistor RM to ground that sets the match; input impedance is then RG ∥ RM. The source impedance enters the noise gain, so the –2 example with RM = 67 Ω has NG = 2.8 and a little less bandwidth than the noninverting G = 2 circuit. RB on the noninverting input, set to the dc resistance seen from the inverting node, cuts the bias-current output error to IOS × RF. Below 350 Ω RB needs no bypass capacitor because its noise is under the amplifier's own; RB must be at least 50 Ω, since a direct short at the noninverting input lets parasitics peak and risks very high-frequency oscillation of the input stage.

Range is set by noise, distortion and parasitic capacitance. A unity-gain follower uses a 25-Ω feedback resistor, not a short, so the output pin is decoupled from the capacitance at the inverting input and the response stays flat. For G > 1, RF is normally 200 Ω to 1.5 kΩ; below 200 Ω the feedback network loads the output and harmonic distortion worsens. Keep RF ∥ RG under about 300 Ω; at high gains RF can then reach several kΩ, provided the pole of RF with its parallel parasitic capacitance stays out of band.

With no load at 25 °C the output swings within 1 V of either rail; into 15 Ω, the minimum tested load, it delivers more than ±160 mA. Taking voltage and current together, inside a 1-W internal dissipation limit, it drives ±2.5 V into 25 Ω or ±3.5 V into 50 Ω, and a 100-Ω load gets the full ±3.9 V. The minimum over-temperature output figures come from worst-case simulations at the cold extreme; in steady operation the output transistors run warmer, swing further and supply more current. Short-circuit protection limits source or sink current to about 250 mA.

A capacitive load on the output pin, such as an ADC input, adds a pole with the open-loop output resistance and reduces phase margin. The simplest fix for flat response, clean pulses and low distortion is a series resistor RS between the output and the load, which adds a compensating zero; choose it from the recommended RS vs capacitive load curves for the flattest, widest response at the load and place it at the output pin. Parasitic loads above 2 pF can start to degrade performance. Because the G = 2 response is already slightly peaked, fairly large RS values are needed; raising the noise gain reduces the RS needed.

Distortion improves directly with load impedance, and the load includes the feedback network (RF + RG noninverting, RF inverting). A 0.1-µF capacitor across the supply pins in bipolar operation improves 2nd-order distortion. The output stage keeps the 2nd- and 3rd-harmonic levels relative to the fundamental roughly constant as output rises, up to about 4 VPP, and intermodulation spurs do not grow as a fixed intercept would predict. With two tones about 20 MHz at 10 dBm per tone into a matched 50-Ω load (8 VPP envelope at the pin), 3rd-order spurs are 47 dBc down; lower frequencies do better.

Input voltage noise and the two input current noises add in root-sum-square fashion with the thermal noise of the source and feedback resistors. With source impedance and RF ∥ RG both under 300 Ω, the total input-referred noise stays close to the amplifier's own; resistor noise is then small enough that RB in the inverting circuit needs no bypass.

The input stage draws relatively high bias current, typically ±8 µA per input, but the two match closely, so equal dc source resistances at both inputs reduce the error to IOS × RF. Most offset trims come down to forcing a dc current through RF: for a noninverting signal path apply the trim as an inverting summing input; for an inverting path the noninverting input can be used, though its dc voltage on the summing junction drives current back into the source, and trim applied at the inverting input can alter noise gain and flatness. Feeding the trim current through resistors much larger than the signal-path resistors leaves the loop gain almost unchanged.

Under extreme conditions heat sinking or airflow can be needed. Dissipation is quiescent power plus output-stage power; the power in the output stage, not in the load, sets it. The worst case is a load that forces current into the output at positive voltages, or draws it out at negative voltages, putting high current across a large internal drop; the output V-I curve shows the 1-W boundary for this. A SOT-23 part at 85 °C ambient driving a grounded 20-Ω load in the dc-coupled G = 2 circuit reaches about 142 °C, under the maximum, though reliability may call for lower junction temperatures.

Direct digital synthesis DACs need a low-distortion output amplifier to keep their SFDR into real loads. One of the two complementary outputs drives the summing junction of a transimpedance stage with dc gain RF; CF across RF cancels the noise-gain peaking from the DAC capacitance.

The 5-MHz Sallen-Key low-pass is biased at midsupply for widest dynamic range; ac coupling of the input and gain resistor makes it a band-pass with a 32-kHz low corner. At a gain of 4 on a single supply the amplifier has roughly 80 MHz of bandwidth, and the filter values allow for it.
The large swing and high current let the part drive a 50-Ω line with up to 4 VPP at the load, 8 VPP at the output, from one 12-V supply.

Intended for ±2.5 V to ±6 V. Put 0.1-µF high-frequency decoupling within 0.1 inch of the supply pins, usually with a larger capacitor (2.2 µF typical) that can sit farther away and be shared among nearby parts. On a single supply only the positive rail needs them; on split supplies decouple each rail to ground. Avoid narrow supply and ground traces. An optional capacitor across the two supplies improves 2nd-harmonic distortion.

Keep parasitic capacitance from the signal pins to ac ground low: at the output and inverting input it threatens stability, while at the noninverting input it forms an unwanted low-pass with the source impedance. Open the ground and power planes around the signal pins and keep them unbroken elsewhere. Put 0.1-µF decoupling within 0.25 inch of the supply pins and 2.2-µF to 6.8-µF capacitors farther off. Use low-reactance resistors (surface-mount best; metal-film or carbon axial also work; never wire-wound), and place the feedback and output series resistors right at the output pin; with double-sided assembly the feedback resistor can go under the package between output and inverting input. Good resistors carry about 0.2 pF in shunt, so values above 1.5 kΩ put a pole or zero under 500 MHz; 402 Ω is a good starting feedback value, 25 Ω for a follower. For short connections treat the trace and next input as a lumped capacitive load and use 50 to 100 mil (1.27 to 2.54 mm) traces with planes cleared, setting RS from the RS vs load curves; loads under 5 pF may need no RS since the part is compensated for 2 pF, and higher gains tolerate more. Long runs can be matched microstrip or stripline with series and shunt terminations (6-dB loss), or series-terminated at the source only; a 50-Ω environment is not needed on board, and higher impedance improves distortion. Do not socket the part; solder it.

Ground and power planes stay on inner layers but are removed under pins 1 and 4 to cut stray capacitance. Bypass capacitors sit close to the power pins, the output resistor close to the output pin, the input resistor close to pin 4, and the feedback resistor on the bottom of the board between pins 4 and 6.
SPICE models predict small-signal ac and transient behaviour well over a wide range of conditions, but harmonic distortion and dG/dP less well, and they do not distinguish between packages.
